newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia tells Timor bishop to avoid politics.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia tells Timor bishop to avoid politics.

text.p: Indonesia has said East Timor's Nobel laureate Bishop Carlos Belo should stay out of politics, the official Antara news agency said on Sunday.

"The Indonesian government has always recognised and respected Bishop Belo in his position as leader of the Catholic Church in East Timor but takes strong exception (to) him engaging in politics," Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas was quoted by the news agency as saying.
"We object to him engaging in politics. That is not what the Vatican expects him to do in his position as bishop of Dili," Alatas said.
Alatas, speaking to reporters in Rome after a meeting with his Vatican counterpart, Archbishop Jean-Louis Tauran, said Indonesia's stance was fully supported by the Vatican.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 and declared the former Portuguese colony its 27th province in July the following year in an act not recognised by the United Nations.

Belo, who last month jointly won the 1996 Nobel Peace prize with self-exiled East Timorese independence movement leader Jose Ramos-Horta, reports directly to the Vatican and only takes part in the activities of the Indonesian Catholic church as an observer.

Alatas said that Belo had given an undertaking to only visit Norway next month to accept his prize and warned the bishop not to let the prize presentation be "used by Belo or other parties to undermine Indonesia".
The Norgewian embassy in Jakarta said on Saturday Belo had been issued a visa last week while he was in Jakarta.
Belo came under fire in Indonesia last week following the circulation of comments he reportedly made to a German magazine in which he said Indonesia had treated East Timorese like "scabby dogs".

After criticism of Belo by senior Indonesian government officials and protest demonstrations against him in Jakarta, youths in East Timor rallied around the bishop and held five days of demonstrations in support of the influential civilian leader.

The demonstrations climaxed with a gathering of more than 60,000 people in Dili on Saturday at Dili's cathedral after the bishop returned from a five-day visit to Jakarta. They peacefully dispersed after Belo told them to stop demonstrating and go home.
Residents said on Sunday Dili had returned to normal and there were no demonstrations or gatherings. One resident said Belo said mass in his residence as was his normal practice on Sunday morning.
